analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over oil and gas drilling permits on federal land, skipping federal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill to let states take over federal oil and gas permitting never came to a vote; it died in the House Natural Resources Committee after a single 2017 subcommittee hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any state apply to take over from the federal government the leasing, permitting, and regulation of oil and gas development on federal land within that state. Once a state's plan is approved, drilling on that land would no longer be subject to the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, or federal historic-preservation review. Royalties would stay the same and go to the same federal accounts, so the main change would be who reviews and approves drilling — state regulators instead of federal ones, with far fewer environmental checks.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that drill or want to drill on federal land. The bill's own findings cite an average of 220 days to process a federal drilling permit and a 31% drop in federal acres leased since 2008; shifting permitting to state agencies would speed approvals and remove federal environmental review, Endangered Species Act consultation, and public participation requirements from each drilling decision. States that opt in would gain regulatory control over drilling on federal land within their borders and could keep application processing fees.

how_it_helps.text: State agencies would take over leasing and permitting of oil and gas on 'available Federal land' — land already identified for oil and gas leasing in federal land-management plans, excluding national parks, wildlife refuges, congressionally designated wilderness, and tribal trust land.

Once a state program is approved, state permitting actions would expressly not count as federal actions under the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Endangered Species Act, or the National Environmental Policy Act — removing environmental review and public comment from drilling decisions.

A state's program would be automatically approved unless, within 60 days, the Interior and Agriculture Secretaries affirmatively find it would cut federal royalties or lacks capability — putting the burden on the federal government to reject rather than on the state to qualify.
The bill cites federal permitting delays (an average of 220 days to process a drilling permit application in 2015) as the problem it aims to fix.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near federal land open to drilling, and the broader public that owns that land. Each drilling project would skip the environmental impact review and public comment process federal law now requires, and federal agencies would lose the ability to protect endangered or threatened species on that land. The Interior and Agriculture Departments could only reject a state plan on narrow grounds (royalty loss or lack of capability), not on environmental grounds. Federal royalty collections would be preserved at the same amounts, so the treasury would not directly lose money.

drawbacks.text: State drilling decisions would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, meaning no environmental impact review and no public comment period before drilling on land owned by all Americans.
State permitting would be exempt from the Endangered Species Act, removing federal protection for threatened and endangered species on federal land opened to drilling.

The 60-day default-approval mechanism means federal agencies could only block a state takeover by proving lost royalties or lack of capability — environmental and public-health concerns would not be valid grounds for rejection.

A supporter would answer that states already run their own oil and gas regulatory programs with enforcement sanctions, and that federal permitting delays of 220 days per application cost companies and state economies without improving environmental outcomes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The efficiency argument is real — federal permitting on federal land is slow, and the bill preserves royalty payments at federal rates and federal accounts, so the treasury is kept whole. But the trade is heavily one-sided: the speed comes from eliminating the review processes — environmental analysis, public comment, and endangered-species consultation — that are the public's main say over drilling on land the public owns. A narrower bill could have set permitting deadlines while keeping federal review; this bill instead routes around it entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which held one hearing in September 2017; it was never marked up, never voted on, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Diane Black introduced the bill on July 28, 2017, with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
The bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on August 14, 2017; the subcommittee held a hearing on September 6, 2017, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a markup or a vote in the House or Senate, and expired at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public kept federal environmental review, public comment, and Endangered Species Act protections for drilling on federal land; oil and gas companies still have to obtain federal permits rather than faster state ones. No one lost anything except the bill's sponsors, who gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Diane Black
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine original cosponsors.

for.name: 12 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 12 were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never reported the bill out; after a subcommittee hearing on September 6, 2017, no markup or vote was scheduled for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Rob Bishop
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or floor vote during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; on sponsorship the bill was entirely Republican — a Republican sponsor and 12 Republican cosponsors, with no Democrats.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land
industries.note: The bill would give these companies state-issued permits instead of federal ones, cutting the average 220-day federal permitting time and exempting each project from environmental review, public comment, and Endangered Species Act consultation. Its gain is the public's loss of oversight over drilling on federally owned land, though federal royalties would be unchanged.

industries.industry: Federal onshore energy regulatory apparatus (BLM and Forest Service permitting)
industries.note: States that opt in would take over leasing and permitting that the Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service now conduct, shrinking the federal role on available federal land. Federal agencies would retain only a narrow check tied to royalty collections and state capability.
